# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/UniHelper.sol#L68-L74


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If `tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]` is negative and `((tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]) % int56(int256(ago)) != 0)`, then returned `tick` will be bigger than it should be  which places operations requiring prices to be right not be able to achieve this goal.

As such, in the case where  `TWAP` is required, then protocol would work with a `flawed prices` since the returned price would be different than it really is, potentially leading to say for example some positions that should be `liquidatable` not being liquidated because before liquidation there is a check to see if the loan is `healthy`. 

Now this check queries the value of this asset via `getSqrtTWAP()` and if returned price is wrong then `unhealthy` loans could be pronounced as `healthy` and vice versa.

## Proof of Concept
In `UniHelper` contract, [getSqrtTWAP()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/UniHelper.sol#L20-L22) function is used by protocol to get `average price`.
```solidity
    function getSqrtTWAP(address uniswapPoolAddress) internal view returns (uint160 sqrtTwapX96) {
        (sqrtTwapX96,) = callUniswapObserve(IUniswapV3Pool(uniswapPoolAddress), _ORACLE_PERIOD);
    }
```

This calls [callUniswapObserve()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/UniHelper.sol#L68-L74) which actually performs the price calculation:
```solidity
        //...
        int56[] memory tickCumulatives = abi.decode(data, (int56[]));

        int24 tick = int24((tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]) / int56(int256(ago)));

        uint160 sqrtPriceX96 = TickMath.getSqrtRatioAtTick(tick);

        return (sqrtPriceX96, ago);
```
It is required that if `tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]` is negative, then `tick` should be rounded down like in [Uniswap library](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-periphery/blob/697c2474757ea89fec12a4e6db16a574fe259610/contracts/libraries/OracleLibrary.sol#L36).

However, this is not done. As result, if `tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]` is negative and `(tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]) % int56(int256(ago)) != 0)`, `tick` will be bigger then it should be. Which opens possibility for arbitrage opportunities.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`tick` should be rounded down in this case:
```diff
    int24 tick = int24((tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]) / int56(int256(ago)));
+  if ((tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]) < 0 && ((tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]) % int56(int256(ago)) != 0)) tick--;
```

















## Assessed type

Uniswap

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/ScaledAsset.sol#L67


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A user could be DoSed  if `finalWithdrawAmount` exceeds the available collateral in the protocol. This is because the `require(getAvailableCollateralValue(tokenState) >= finalWithdrawAmount, "S0");` check will revert the transaction, preventing the user from withdrawing their assets.

## Proof of Concept
[withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/PredyPool.sol#L242) calls [removeAsset()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/ScaledAsset.sol#L67) function which allows users to withdraw assets from the protocol.
It calculates the `finalBurnAmount` and `finalWithdrawAmount` based on the user's request and the current state of the protocol.

Before allowing the withdrawal, the function checks if the available collateral is sufficient to cover the `finalWithdrawAmount`:
```solidity
require(getAvailableCollateralValue(tokenState) >= finalWithdrawAmount, "S0");
```
The [getAvailableCollateralValue()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/ScaledAsset.sol#L226-L228) returns the diffrence between total deposited collateral and total borrows:
```solidity
    function getAvailableCollateralValue(AssetStatus memory tokenState) internal pure returns (uint256) {
        return getTotalCollateralValue(tokenState) - getTotalDebtValue(tokenState);
    }
```
As seen, if the available collateral is less than the `finalWithdrawAmount`, the transaction reverts with the error `"S0"`.

This means the user cannot proceed with the withdrawal, effectively locking their assets in the protocol.
This situation can occur if the protocol's collateral is heavily utilized.

Therefore, the user will be forced to perform another withdrawal attempt with the hopes that it would succeed this time. However, there's no such guarantees as there are chances that there still won't be enough collateral to cover for his withdraw amount. 

Combined with the fact that he may not be the only user trying to withdraw their funds, this situation can stick indefinitely. 

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Allow partial withdrawals if the full amount cannot be withdrawn. This can be achieved by adjusting the `finalWithdrawAmount` to the available collateral.












## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/LiquidationLogic.sol#L49-L53


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The protocol does not pause `interest` payments while an unsafe vault is liquidated. As such, `interest` continues to accrue and is updated even during liquidation.

## Vulnerability Details
The liquidation process involves checking if the `vault` is in danger, executing the liquidation trade, and adjusting the vault's margin based on the trade result.

The `interest` is updated right before the liquidation process begins. This means that the vault's position continues to accrue `interest` up to the point of liquidation.
This can be seen in the following lines in [liquidate()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/LiquidationLogic.sol#L49-L53) function:
```solidity
    // update interest growth
    ApplyInterestLib.applyInterestForToken(globalData.pairs, vault.openPosition.pairId);

    // update rebalance interest growth
    Perp.updateRebalanceInterestGrowth(pairStatus, pairStatus.sqrtAssetStatus);
```
The liquidation process checks if the `vault` is in danger using the [checkVaultIsDanger()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/LiquidationLogic.sol#L55-L57) function.
If the vault is deemed `liquidatable`, the [Trade.trade()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/LiquidationLogic.sol#L67) function is called to execute the liquidation trade.
The `vault`'s `margin` is then adjusted based on the trade result, which includes the updated `interest` values.

---> The `vault` continues to accrue `interest` up to the point of liquidation, which may lead to additional penalties for the liquidated position.
This can be unfair to the vault owner, as the liquidation process itself should ideally halt any further interest accrual.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement logic to `pause interest accrual` for positions flagged for liquidation. This ensures that no `additional interest` is accrued once the liquidation process begins.


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/PredyPool.sol#L222-L228


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
There is no way for protocol to selectively disable `deposits` and `borrows` from a `pool`. Without the ability to selectively disable certain actions like deposits and borrows, the protocol might face increased risks during periods of market volatility or hack. 

Users might rush to deposit assets or borrow against them, potentially leading to over-leveraged positions that could trigger liquidations if the market moves unfavorably. 

## Vulnerability Details
Commonly in lending platforms, when a certain `token` or `lending pool` has been deemed to be too risky or have been hacked, it is `retired`. This means that all `deposits` and `borrows` from the pool are stopped, however the pool is kept in the system for users to withdraw and repay their loans.
This is a common feature and is a good way to deleverage the system from risky assets while prventing users from being locked out of thei funds.

This has happened multiple times in `AAve` with some other examples below:
- `GHST` & `agEUR` borrowing disbaled on Polygon
- `UST`, `TRXOld` & `SXP` disbaled on Venus protocol on BSC

The main idea being that protocols often delist tokens, and they do that by disabling deposits and borrows, but still allow users to withdraw and repay their loans.

---> The issue is that this functionality does not exist in this protocol.

Consider the [supply()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/PredyPool.sol#L222-L228) function:
```solidity
    function supply(uint256 pairId, bool isQuoteAsset, uint256 supplyAmount)
        external
        nonReentrant
        returns (uint256 finalSuppliedAmount)
    {
        return SupplyLogic.supply(globalData, pairId, supplyAmount, isQuoteAsset);
    }
```
As seen here, the supply of tokens into these pools cannot be halted by any means.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Have a `retire` option in the lending pool which can be used to disable deposits and borrows.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/base/SettlementCallbackLib.sol#L99-L108
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/base/SettlementCallbackLib.sol#L146-L155


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `sell()` and `buy()` functions in the `SettlementCallbackLib` library have incorrect token transfer logic when `settlementParams.contractAddress == address(0)`. This results in the user supplying and receiving the wrong tokens during direct fills.

## Proof of Concept
When selling, the user should:
- Supply `baseToken`.
- Receive `quoteToken`.
However, the opposite is done in [sell()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/base/SettlementCallbackLib.sol#L99-L108):
```solidity
    if (settlementParams.contractAddress == address(0)) {
            // direct fill
            uint256 quoteAmount = sellAmount * price / Constants.Q96;

            predyPool.take(false, sender, sellAmount); // @audit-issue User receives baseToken

            ERC20(quoteToken).safeTransferFrom(sender, address(predyPool), quoteAmount); @audit-issue User supplies quoteToken

            return;
        }
```


When buying, the user should:
- Supply `quoteToken`.
- Receive `baseToken`.
However, the opposite is done in [buy()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/base/SettlementCallbackLib.sol#L146-L155):
```solidity
    if (settlementParams.contractAddress == address(0)) {
            // direct fill
            uint256 quoteAmount = buyAmount * price / Constants.Q96;

            predyPool.take(true, sender, quoteAmount); // @audit-issue User receives quoteToken

            ERC20(baseToken).safeTransferFrom(sender, address(predyPool), buyAmount); // @audit-issue User supplies baseToken

            return;
        }
```
As seen, the whole logic is incorrect resulting incorrect trade executions.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Correct this as follows:

`sell()`
```solidity
uint256 quoteAmount = sellAmount * price / Constants.Q96;
predyPool.take(true, sender, quoteAmount); // @audit User takes quote tokens
ERC20(baseToken).safeTransferFrom(sender, address(predyPool), sellAmount); // @audit User supplies base tokens
````

`buy()`
```solidity
uint256 baseAmount = buyAmount * price / Constants.Q96;
predyPool.take(true, sender, baseAmount ); // @audit User takes baseToken
ERC20(quoteToken).safeTransferFrom(sender, address(predyPool), buyAmount); // @audit User supplies quoteToken
````

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/gamma/GammaTradeMarket.sol#L444-L455


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
By design, with `permit` calls, the token ignores the `msg.sender`. Combined with the fact TXs can be observed in the `mempool` (by anyone, or at least by the sequencer in some L2s), it means that a `permit` can be easily frontran (simply duplicate the TX arguments).

The user's execution will be `reverted`, forcing the user to formulate the commands, thus spending in another transaction.

## Proof of Concept
The `_permit2.permitWitnessTransferFrom()` command is intended to allow off-chain signed approvals to be used on-chain, saving gas and improving user experience.

This is used in [_verifyOrder()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/gamma/GammaTradeMarket.sol#L444-L455):
```solidity
    function _verifyOrder(ResolvedOrder memory order) internal {
        order.validate();


        _permit2.permitWitnessTransferFrom(
            order.toPermit(),
            order.transferDetails(address(this)),
            order.info.trader,
            order.hash,
            GammaOrderLib.PERMIT2_ORDER_TYPE,
            order.sig
        );
    }
```
The actual verification is done [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/lib/permit2/src/SignatureTransfer.sol#L60-L67):
```solidity
        if (block.timestamp > permit.deadline) revert SignatureExpired(permit.deadline);
        if (requestedAmount > permit.permitted.amount) revert InvalidAmount(permit.permitted.amount);


        _useUnorderedNonce(owner, permit.nonce);


        signature.verify(_hashTypedData(dataHash), owner);


        ERC20(permit.permitted.token).safeTransferFrom(owner, transferDetails.to, requestedAmount);
```
This function transfers tokens using a signed permit messages.

###### But what if an `attacker` extracts the `permit` parameters from the call and frontruns it with a direct `permit()` ? 

In this case, the end result is harmful, since the user loses the functionality that follows the `permit()`.

Including this command in a call to `executeTrade()` will make the transaction susceptible to `DOS` via `frontrunning`. 

An `attacker` can observe the transaction in the mempool, extract the `permit signature` and values from the calldata and execute the permit before the original transaction is processed.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider implementing a mechanism to check if an allowance for the desired amount exists in case the call to `permit()` fails.













## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/2fb1e0ec7a52fc06c2e9c8e561bccba84302e4bb/src/PredyPool.sol#L68
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/2fb1e0ec7a52fc06c2e9c8e561bccba84302e4bb/src/base/BaseHookCallbackUpgradable.sol#L13

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the contracts that implement `Openzeppelin`’s `Upgreadable` model, uninitialized `Implementation` contract can be taken over by an attacker with `initialize()` function.

## Proof of Concept
###### Scenario:
1. `Proxy` & `Implementation` are deployed.
2. The `Proxy` delegates calls to `Implementation.initialize()` which sets the `owner` and switches `initialized` to `true` in the state of the `Proxy`.
3. The storage of `Implementation` however is still intact e.g `owner` is unset and `initialized` is `false`.
4. An attacker calls `initialize()` directly on `Implementation` and sets himself as the `owner`.
5. From here, he has full control to perform any maliceous activities.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
From [Openzeppelin Docs](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/upgrades-plugins/1.x/writing-upgradeable):


*Do not leave an implementation contract uninitialized. An uninitialized implementation contract can be taken over by an attacker, which may impact the proxy. To prevent the implementation contract from being used, you should invoke the _disableInitializers function in the constructor to automatically lock it when it is deployed*:

```diff
-   constructor() {}
+   constructor() {
        _disableInitializers();
    }
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/settlements/UniswapSettlement.sol#L34
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/settlements/UniswapSettlement.sol#L50


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The protocol is using `block.timestamp` as the `deadline` argument while performing swaps, which completely defeats the purpose of using a `deadline`.

Failure to provide a proper `deadline` value enables pending transactions to be maliciously executed at a later point. Transactions that provide an insufficient amount of gas such that they are not mined within a reasonable amount of time, can be picked by `malicious actors` or `MEV` bots and executed later in detriment of the submitter.

## Proof of Concept
[swapExactIn](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/settlements/UniswapSettlement.sol#L33-L35)
```solidity
        amountOut = _swapRouter.exactInput(
            ISwapRouter.ExactInputParams(data, recipient, block.timestamp, amountIn, amountOutMinimum)
        );
```

[swapExactOut](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/settlements/UniswapSettlement.sol#L49-L51)
```solidity
        amountIn = _swapRouter.exactOutput(
            ISwapRouter.ExactOutputParams(data, recipient, block.timestamp, amountOut, amountInMaximum)
        );
```
Using `block.timestamp` as the `deadline` is effectively a no-operation that has no effect nor protection. Since `block.timestamp` will take the timestamp value when the transaction gets mined, the check will end up comparing `block.timestamp` against the same value.

See [this](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-periphery/blob/697c2474757ea89fec12a4e6db16a574fe259610/contracts/base/PeripheryValidation.sol#L7).

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Include a check to ensure that the current `block.timestamp` is less than or equal to the `deadline` specified in the parameters. If the current timestamp is greater than the `deadline`, the function should `revert` the transaction.





## Assessed type

Timing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/2fb1e0ec7a52fc06c2e9c8e561bccba84302e4bb/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L206


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `currentSqrtPrice` is used in `Perp.reallocate()` to perform swap if the current tick is out of range. 

However this is calculated based on the `current pool price` i.e (`IUniswapV3Pool(_sqrtAssetStatus.uniswapPool).slot0()`), which can be manipulated and since the `swap` is performed based on this value, it can be manipulated as well resulting in incorrect `swap amounts`.

## Proof of Concept
Under the hood this function fetches the [current price](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/2fb1e0ec7a52fc06c2e9c8e561bccba84302e4bb/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L206) in the pool:

```solidity
        (uint160 currentSqrtPrice, int24 currentTick,,,,,) = IUniswapV3Pool(_sqrtAssetStatus.uniswapPool).slot0();
```
Based on this value, [swap](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/2fb1e0ec7a52fc06c2e9c8e561bccba84302e4bb/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L253-L257) is performed if the current tick is out of range: 
```solidity
        // if the current tick is out of range, then swap
        if (isOutOfRange) {
            (deltaPositionBase, deltaPositionQuote) =
                swapForOutOfRange(_assetStatusUnderlying, currentSqrtPrice, tick, totalLiquidityAmount);
        }
```
If a malicious user decides to distort the pool price in the current block (through a `flash loan` for example), this will directly impact the calculated value.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use `TWAP` to get the value of `currentSqrtPrice` rather than `slot0()`

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L32-L33
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L65-L66


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Each time a user interacts with the contract the following two functions comes to play:
1. [applyInterestForToken()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/ApplyInterestLib.sol#L26-L48): Here, interest and premium from the previous interaction to the current one are applied.
2. [updateRebalanceInterestGrowth()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L158-L174): This settles the interest on rebalance positions up to this block and update the rebalance fee growth value.

Both of these are invoked within functions such as `liquidate()`, `reallocate()` and  `trade()`.

However, in `supply()` and `withdraw()`, only `applyInterestForToken()` is called to update `interest growth` whereas `updateRebalanceInterestGrowth()` is not. 

As such, `rebalance interest growth` is never updated during these operations.

## Proof of Concept
In [liquidate()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/LiquidationLogic.sol#L49-L53), [reallocate()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/ReallocationLogic.sol#L34-L40) and [trade()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/TradeLogic.sol#L36-L40), both two functions are invoked:
```solidity
        // update interest growth
        ApplyInterestLib.applyInterestForToken(globalData.pairs, vault.openPosition.pairId);


        // update rebalance interest growth
        Perp.updateRebalanceInterestGrowth(pairStatus, pairStatus.sqrtAssetStatus);
```
These ensure that both `interest growth` and `rebalance interest growth` are updated up to the current block.

However, in `supply()` and `withdraw()`, only `applyInterestForToken()` is invoked.
[supply()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L32-L33)
```solidity
        // Updates interest rate related to the pair
        ApplyInterestLib.applyInterestForToken(globalData.pairs, _pairId);
```

[withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L65-L66)
```solidity
        // Updates interest rate related to the pair
        ApplyInterestLib.applyInterestForToken(globalData.pairs, _pairId);
```
As seen above, `rebalance interest growth` is never updated during these operations. This means that any interests on rebalance positions are never settled  and fees never updated. 

Subsequent operations that follow any supply or withdrawal are then done with outdated interest and fee updates as these were omitted prior. 

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Modify the `supply()` and `withdraw()` functions to update both interest growth and rebalance interest growth.
```diff
        // update interest growth
        ApplyInterestLib.applyInterestForToken(globalData.pairs, _pairId);

+       // update rebalance interest growth
+       Perp.updateRebalanceInterestGrowth(pairStatus, pairStatus.sqrtAssetStatus);
```





















## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/perp/PerpMarketLib.sol#L183-L185


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `ratio()` function in `PerpMarketLib` is designed to calculate the percentage difference between two prices, scaled by a constant `Bps.ONE`. 
However, the issue here lies in the inconsistency of the `denominator` used when `price1` is less than `price2`.

This yields an incorrect value. 

## Proof of Concept
Here is the [ratio()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/perp/PerpMarketLib.sol#L178-L186) function:
```solidity
function ratio(uint256 price1, uint256 price2) internal pure returns (uint256) {
    if (price1 == price2) {
        return 0;
    } else if (price1 > price2) {
        return (price1 - price2) * Bps.ONE / price2;
    } else {
        return (price2 - price1) * Bps.ONE / price2;
    }
}
```
When `price1 < price2`, the function uses `price2` as the `denominator`. 
```solidity
        } else {
            return (price2 - price1) * Bps.ONE / price2;
        }
```
This is inconsistent with the case where `price1 > price2`, which uses `price2` as the `denominator`.

#### Breakdown
With the current implementation:

1. `if (price1 > price2)`
Here, ratio = `(price1 - price2) * Bps.ONE / price2;`
Example: Let price1 = 10e6, price2 = 5e6, Bps.ONE = 1e6
Then:
```solidity
ratio = (10e6 - 5e6) * 1e6 / 5e6 = 1e6
```

2. `if (price2 > price1)`
Here, ratio = `(price2 - price1) * Bps.ONE / price2;`
Example: Let price2 = 10e6, price1 = 5e6, Bps.ONE = 1e6
Then:
```solidity
ratio = (10e6 - 5e6) * 1e6 / 10e6 = 5e5
```
The `ratio` calculated in the first instance is`1e6` but the second case yields `5e5`. This is incorrect since the wrong `denominator` is used here i.e (`price2`).

The `ratio()` function is then used in [validateStopPrice()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/perp/PerpMarketLib.sol#L147-L153) to calculate `decayedSlippageTorelance`:
```solidity
        uint256 decayedSlippageTorelance = DecayLib.decay2(
            auctionParams.startPrice,
            auctionParams.endPrice,
            auctionParams.startTime,
            auctionParams.endTime,
  @>        ratio(oraclePrice, stopPrice) // @audit-issue ratio used here
        );
``` 
From this, the whole calculation will be flawed.
 
## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The `denominator` in the `else` block should be `price1` instead of `price2` to maintain a consistent approach to calculating the `ratio`.
```diff
        } else {
-           return (price2 - price1) * Bps.ONE / price2;
+           return (price2 - price1) * Bps.ONE / price1;
        }
```

i.e 
`if (price2 > price1)`
Here, ratio should be: `(price2 - price1) * Bps.ONE / price1;`
Example: Let price2 = 10e6, price1 = 5e6, Bps.ONE = 1e6
Then:
```solidity
ratio = (10e6 - 5e6) * 1e6 / 5e6 = 1e6
```
The `ratio` returned is now consistent in both cases.

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/orders/DecayLib.sol#L16


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
When the `decayEndTime` is before the `current time`, then it might be wrong.

If the `decay()` function is invoked to calculate a price when the decay period has ended, this could produce misleading results. For example, using wrong/unintended `decayEndTime` and expecting the function to return a meaningful decayed price based on the current time would not yield accurate outcomes.

## Proof of Concept
The [decay()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/orders/DecayLib.sol#L21-L22) function only performs the following check:
```solidity
        if (decayEndTime < decayStartTime) {
            revert EndTimeBeforeStartTime();
```
However, it does not verify that the `decayEndTime` provided is indeed in the future.

This `decay()` function is used in [validateMarketOrder()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/perp/PerpMarketLib.sol#L195-L197) to fetch `decayedPrice ` associated with some `AuctionParams`:

```solidity
        uint256 decayedPrice = DecayLib.decay(
            auctionParams.startPrice, auctionParams.endPrice, auctionParams.startTime, auctionParams.endTime
        );
```
If the `decay()` function does not verify that `auctionParams.endTime` is a future timestamp, then the returned value, (`decayedPrice`) will by all means be incorrect.

## Impact
With this incorrect value returned, the market order may be [validated wrongly](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/perp/PerpMarketLib.sol#L199-L209):
```solidity
        if (tradeAmount != 0) {
            if (tradeAmount > 0 && decayedPrice < tradePrice) { // @audit-issue The value used here
                return false;
            }


            if (tradeAmount < 0 && decayedPrice > tradePrice) { // @audit-issue The value used here
                return false;
            }
        }


        return true;
```
From this, the whole validation relies on the `decayedPrice` returned and as such, if this value is incorrect, the whole validation is incorrect.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Therefore, the system should include a sanity check to ensure `decayEndTime > block.timestamp`.

Add the following check:

```solidity
if (decayEndTime <= block.timestamp) revert EndTimeLessThanCurrentTime();
```








## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L237
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L222


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The lack of a slippage mechanism in supply and withdraw functions could result in bad trade



## Proof of Concept
In the `PredyPool` contract, both `supply` and `withdraw` methods lack a slippage mechanism, which can lead to unfavorable trades for users.
```solidity
    function supply(uint256 pairId, bool isQuoteAsset, uint256 supplyAmount)
        external
        nonReentrant
        returns (uint256 finalSuppliedAmount)
    {
        return SupplyLogic.supply(globalData, pairId, supplyAmount, isQuoteAsset);
    }

    function withdraw(uint256 pairId, bool isQuoteAsset, uint256 withdrawAmount)
        external
        nonReentrant
        returns (uint256 finalBurnAmount, uint256 finalWithdrawAmount)
    {
        return SupplyLogic.withdraw(globalData, pairId, withdrawAmount, isQuoteAsset);
    }
```

Here’s how the lack of slippage can be exploited:

1. User A wants to supply 100,000,000 USDC and expects a corresponding number of bond shares. However, User's B supply tx executed before User A's supply transaction and deposit a large number of assets, which will significantly increase `tokenState.assetScaler` and decrease the number of bond shares for User A. As `tokenState.assetScale` increase based on the utilization i.e deposit , withdrawal and trade and inversely proportional to bond shares wrt supplied asset

2. A similar scenario can occur during withdrawals.

Slippage is a crucial parameter when adding or withdrawing assets from such vaults/pools to protect users from these kinds of attacks/losses
## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a mechanism to specify the expected number of bond shares a lender expects from supplying assets, and similarly, the expected amount of assets from a withdrawal. This will protect users from significant changes in the `tokenState.assetScaler` due to front-running or other manipulations.





## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/PriceFeed.sol#L45-L58
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/LiquidationLogic.sol#L39


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Traders are prone to liquidation when an L2 sequencer becomes online as there is no grace period for traders to adjust their positions.

## Proof of Concept
Please read this section of the [blog](https://dacian.me/lending-borrowing-defi-attacks#heading-borrower-immediately-liquidated-after-repayments-resume) -

>However one more issue remains; if repayments are paused, during that pause market fluctuations can cause a Borrower to become subject to liquidation as the Borrower is unable to repay(). As soon as repayments are resumed, such a Borrower will be immediately liquidated by liquidation bots, with the only possibility to save their position being if the Borrower themselves runs a repayment bot & can successfully front-run the liquidation bots.

>This situation unfairly disadvantages Borrowers as such Borrowers became subject to liquidation through no fault of their own. Upon repayments resuming a Borrower will be immediately liquidated, unfairly disadvantaging the Borrower and giving a huge advantage to the Liquidator.

>To fix the game theory such that neither Borrowers nor Liquidators are unfairly favored, after repayments are resumed there should be a grace period during which Borrowers can't be liquidated. 

Although the protocol has not directly implemented a pausing functionality. Think of L2 sequencer downtime scenarios. 

When an L2 sequencer comes online again after it went offline, and if the market conditions continue to remain unfavourable for traders, they can get immediately liquidated by bots, as they don't have enough time to adjust their positions.

The protocol should give grace time to traders to avoid liquidations. Put another way, liquidations should only be executed after the grace time has passed.

AAVE has implemented a grace time for its users to avoid liquidations - 
https://docs.aave.com/developers#price-oracle-sentinel

Since the impact of the issue is high and the likelihood can be low, this issue is of medium severity.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a grace time after the L2 sequencer comes back online, such that liquidations can only be executed after the grace time has passed, giving enough time for traders to adjust their margins.


## Assessed type

Other

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/PriceFeed.sol#L45-L58


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The wrong price range will be consumed by the protocol, affecting the trading activity with incorrect prices.

## Proof of Concept
To understand this issue better, please read this section from [Pyth](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/LiquidationLogic.sol#L39) docs:

>The aggregate confidence interval interpolates between the two cases above as publishers’ prices begin to diverge. In situations closer to case 1 where there is significant overlap of the individual publishers’ intervals, the aggregate interval (μ-σ, μ+σ) will capture most of the spread of the individual publishers. In the situation where the prices look more like case 2 with greater disjointness due to different views of the price across different venues, that aggregate interval may be in some eyes an imperfect measure of spread because there may be a number of individual price intervals that lie outside the aggregate interval. In this case, a protocol has a couple of options:

>2.It can decide that there is too much uncertainty when σ/μ exceeds some threshold and choose to pause any new activity that depends on the price of this asset.

During extremely volatile market conditions, the aggregate interval returned by Pyth might not reflect accurate prices. In such circumstances, the publishers do not agree on the aggregate price interval and hence there could be a number of individual price intervals that lie outside the aggregate interval. In such cases, the price interval being consumed will be incorrect.

As the 2nd point suggests, new activity should be paused when such a case happens. Transactions should revert when there is too much uncertainty (when σ/μ exceeds some threshold)

Another protocol consuming Pyth has rightly implemented this [check](https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2023-12-flatmoney-NishithPat/blob/5db084c27199bb2b07cb005f545802c5641e9287/flatcoin-v1/src/OracleModule.sol#L178) -

```solidity
// Check that Pyth price confidence meets minimum
if (priceData.price / int64(priceData.conf)< 
 int32(offchainOracle.minConfidenceRatio)) {
   invalid = true; // price confidence is too low
}
```

## Tools Used
Manual review, Pyth docs

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use the recommendation as suggested above. Check that when σ/μ exceeds some threshold, the transactions do not execute. 





## Assessed type

Oracle

The vulnerability is arises when a contract grants token approval without resetting the previous allowance to zero and  This issue is occurs, where the functions approve a certain amount of tokens for the swap router but do not reset any existing approvals. And  This can lead to the approved amount accumulating over time, creating a vulnerability that malicious actors can exploit to transfer more tokens than intended.

```solidity
function swapExactIn(
    address,

    bytes memory data,
    uint256 amountIn,
    uint256 amountOutMinimum,
    address recipient

    ERC20(baseToken).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amountIn);
    ERC20(baseToken).approve(address(_swapRouter), amountIn);  <—— Vulnerable line

    amountOut = _swapRouter.exactInput(
        ISwapRouter.ExactInputParams(data, recipient, block.timestamp, amountIn, amountOutMinimum)
    );
}
```
In the function swapExactOut

```Solidity 

function swapExactOut(
    address quoteToken,
    address,
    bytes memory data,
    uint256 amountOut,
    uint256 amountInMaximum,
    address recipient
) external override returns (uint256 amountIn) {
    ERC20(quoteToken).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amountInMaximum);
    ERC20(quoteToken).approve(address(_swapRouter), amountInMaximum);  <—- Vulnerable part

    amountIn = _swapRouter.exactOutput(
        ISwapRouter.ExactOutputParams(data, recipient, block.timestamp, amountOut, amountInMaximum)
    );

    if (amountInMaximum > amountIn) {
        ERC20(quoteToken).safeTransfer(msg.sender, amountInMaximum - amountIn);
    }
}

```
It’s that the failure to clear previous token approvals, causing cumulative approvals that can be exploited
## Impact

The over-approval is can lead to unauthorized token transfers, allowing an attacker to repeatedly drain funds from the contract, and  resulting  financial losses for users.

## Proof of Concept
The Uniswap documentation is recommends that contracts should generally reduce the approved allowance to zero before setting a new approval to avoid over-approval issues here 
```solidity
// First reduce the spender's allowance to 0 and then set the desired value:
token.approve(spender, 0);
token.approve(spender, amount);
This prevents lingering approval that might be exploited
```
As scenario of attack : 
- Let’s that Alice has 1000 tokens of BaseToken and 1000 tokens of QuoteToken so The UniswapSettlement contract and a UniswapRouter are set up to facilitate token swaps.
- so  Alice performs a swap using swapExactIn with an initial approval.
- and the  contract approves tokens without resetting previous allowances.
An attacker exploits the remaining approval for unauthorized transactions.
- Alice wants to swap 500 BaseToken for at least 475 tokens of another asset using swapExactIn, Alice transfers 500 BaseToken to the contract.
- The contract approves 500 tokens for the UniswapRouter without resetting any previous approval as result Alice receives 475 tokens and 
The approval of 500 tokens remains active
- now The attacker notices that the approval for BaseToken is still 500 tokens.
- And They can use this approval to initiate a transfer using the UniswapRouter, potentially transferring all 500 tokens that Alice approved, without her knowledge.
- The attacker call a function that utilizes the lingering approval to transfer the remaining tokens
- Alice now wants to swap for an exact amount using swapExactOut. She sets a maximum of 500 QuoteToken
- Alice transfers 500 QuoteToken to the contract.
The contract approves 500 tokens for the UniswapRouter without resetting any previous approval
- Alice swaps her tokens as intended.
- The approval for 500 tokens remains active, and if not fully used, can be exploited similarly
## Tools Used
Manual review 
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It’s need to modify the swapExactIn and swapExactOut functions to reset the approval to zero before setting a new approval amount



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/settlements/UniswapSettlement.sol#L34

# Vulnerability details

## Root of the bug 
The bug is arise from the absence of validation on the data in the `swapExactIn` and `swapExactOut` functions. 
These functions directly pass the data to Uniswap's router without any checks, cause The data is  used for routing swaps in Uniswap's exactInput and exactOutput , is passed without validation.
and This parameter should typically contain the routing path for a swap, specifying the sequence of token pairs involved in the trade. If not validated, a  malicious or malformed data can cause swaps to route through unexpected or harmful paths, resulting in incorrect token transfers or financial losses.

- Here in `swapExactIn` the  data is passed directly to `ISwapRouter.ExactInputParams `without any checks:

```solidity
ISwapRouter.ExactInputParams(data, recipient, block.timestamp, amountIn, amountOutMinimum)
```
- And here in `swapExactOut` also the data is passed directly to `ISwapRouter.ExactOutputParas `without validation: 

```solidity
ISwapRouter.ExactOutputParams(data, recipient, block.timestamp, amountOut, amountInMaximum)
```
## Impact
The issue is can result in unauthorized or incorrect swaps, leading to financial loss
## Proof of Concept

The documentation in the UniswapSettlement contract indicates that critical operations, as swaps, should be carefully managed and controlled by specific actors, and any parameters involved should be securely handled to avoid misuse.
Here : 

```solidity
"Operator/PoolCreator: Currently, the Operator and PoolCreator are the same and hold the admin role in the Predy protocol. Operator can register pairs and PoolCreator can update the parameters of registered pairs."
This implies that functions involving significant operations like swaps should have controlled access and should only be performed by authorized actors to prevent unauthorized use.
```
And here for Parameter Management:

```solidity
"For specific usage, please refer to the Interest Rate Model. PoolOwner specifies the address that can update the pool's settings. PriceFeed specifies the contract that can obtain the oracle price for the pair. If a zero address is specified, the TWAP from the UniswapPool will be used as the oracle price."
This highlights the importance of secure and validated parameters, such as data in swap operations, to avoid exploitation.
```
```solidity
"Register a pair of quoteToken and baseToken. In practice, register the corresponding Uniswap pool with the quoteToken. The token in the Uniswap pool that is not the quoteToken will become the baseToken."
```
- here a scenario show the issue : 
- let’s say that an an attacker, discovers that the data parameter is not validated in the swapExactIn function. And She prepares malicious data that, when used, could route tokens through unintended paths 
- an example of malicious 
` data bytes memory maliciousData = hex"deadbeef"; // Invalid routing path `
- now the attacker sends a transaction to the swapExactIn function with the crafted malicious data as an example :  
```solidity 
uniswapSettlement.swapExactIn(
    address(this),
    baseToken,
    maliciousData,
    1000,
    950,
    address(this)
);
```
- as result The exactInput function receives the malicious data, attempting to execute a swap with an invalid or malicious routing path.
- Since data is not validated, this could result in the swap failing or tokens being routed incorrectly.
the attacker  can exploit this to steal tokens from the contract or execute unintended swaps that could lead to financial loss.
## Tools Used
Manual review 
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It’s need to ensure the data parameter conforms to expected formats and values before processing and it’s better that strict only authorized users can execute these functions

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/BaseMarketUpgradable.sol#L140-L142


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The [filler](https://docs.predy.finance/predy-v6/dev/architecture#filler) of a market is able to update the mapping `_whiteListedSettlements`. This would allow them to manipulate the addresses from the mapping, by leaving it empty or setting a contract of their own, thereby breaking all functions dependent on the functionality of the [SettlementCallbackLib](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/SettlementCallbackLib.sol) contract.

## Proof of Concept

The function `predySettlementCallback` found both in [BaseMarket](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/BaseMarket.sol#L28-L38) and [BaseMarketUpgradable](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/BaseMarketUpgradable.sol#L49-L59) is responsible for multiple things, one of which is validating the settlement address that is passed within the [settlementData](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/BaseMarketUpgradable.sol#L52). The call to [validate](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/SettlementCallbackLib.sol#L29-L38) handles the validation of the address, and if it is invalid, a revert occurs. One of the checks verifies that the passed address is within the [_whiteListedSettlements ](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/BaseMarket.sol#L17) mapping. However, as the function [updateWhitelistSettlement](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/BaseMarketUpgradable.sol#L140-L142) is only access controlled by the [onlyFiller](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/BaseMarketUpgradable.sol#L31-L34) modifier, the filler of the market can just:
- Revoke the `whitelist` of all whitelisted addresses. The end result is: all calls to `predySettlementCallback` reverting and none of the settlements getting executed, leaving the protocol suspended. To accomplish this, the `filler` needs to call the function for every contract in the mapping and set the bool `isEnabled` to false.
- Create a malicious contract, whitelist it, and use it as the only whitelisted settlement address to profit from the settlements.

Please note that the `filler` role is not trusted by the protocol, and the only trusted roles are: `Operator` and `Pool Owner`. The safest option would be for the `Pool Owner` to be the only one with access to `updateWhitelistSettlement`.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

One way to mitigate this issue is by importing Solmate's [Owned](https://github.com/transmissions11/solmate/blob/main/src/auth/Owned.sol) contract and making `BaseMarketUpgradable` inherit from it. Afterwards, swap out the `onlyFiller` modifier for the `onlyOwner` one and make sure to initialize the `Owned` contract in the function [__BaseMarket_init](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/base/BaseMarketUpgradable.sol#L38-L47) in order for the actual owner to be set.

```diff
-    function updateWhitelistSettlement(address settlementContractAddress, bool isEnabled) external onlyFiller {
+    function updateWhitelistSettlement(address settlementContractAddress, bool isEnabled) external onlyOwner {
        _whiteListedSettlements[settlementContractAddress] = isEnabled;
    }
```








## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L222-L228


# Vulnerability details

[PredyPool::supply()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L222C4-L228C6) is used by lenders to provide liquidity either as `quoteToken` or as `baseToken` to the lending pool. In return, they receive bond tokens, which are shares of the pool. The problem is that this function is susceptible to the [Inflation Attack](https://mixbytes.io/blog/overview-of-the-inflation-attack), in which the first depositor can be front-runned by an attacker to steal their deposit.

## Impact

[PredyPool](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol) acts as a vault: accounts deposit some tokens and get back another token (share) that represents their participation in the vault.

These types of contracts are potentially vulnerable to the inflation attack: an attacker can front-run the initial deposit to the vault to inflate the value of a share and render the front-runned deposit worthless.

In this contract, no validation is done in the number of minted tokens. This means that an attacker can execute the attack by front-running the initial deposit. See *Proof of Concept* for a detailed walkthrough of the issue.

## Proof of Concept

The flow is as follows:

- A user registers a new trading pair by calling [PredyPool::registerPair()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L109C4-L111C6).
- To supply liquidity to the newly created pool, the user calls [PredyPool::supply()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L222C4-L228C6) providing the pool's `pairId` and the desired `supplyAmount`.
- This triggers [SupplyLogic::supply()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L22C4-L44C6), which in turn calls [SupplyLogic::receiveTokenAndMintBond()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L46C3-L55C6) These functions work together to mint `bond tokens` to the user and adding liquidity to the pool.

Imagine the following scenario:

1. Bob creates a new trading pair by calling  [PredyPool::registerPair()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L109C4-L111C6).

2. Bob initiates a transaction using [PredyPool::supply()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L222C4-L228C6). He provides the pool's `pairId` and intends to supply `5 WETH` (5e18 worth of tokens). This transaction gets added to the public mempool, which is a temporary storage area for pending transactions.

3. Alice has been monitoring the mempool for profitable opportunities. She sees Bob's transaction and decides to frontrun it. Frontrunning refers to exploiting the fact that transactions aren't processed instantly. Alice submits two transactions before Bob's:

- A [PredyPool::supply()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L222C4-L228C6) call with a minimal amount (`1 wei`) to establish herself as the first liquidity provider. This small contribution grants her a tiny share of the pool.
- A direct transfer of `10 WETH` (10e18 worth of tokens) to the pool contract.

4. Since Alice was the first to call [PredyPool::supply()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L222C4-L228C6), even with a minimal amount, she gets priority in share allocation. This means Bob receives 0 `bond tokens` even though he supplied `5 WETH`.

5. After successfully frontrunning Bob for `bond tokens`, Alice can now withdraw her contributions. She initiates another transaction to withdraw her initial `1 wei`. However, due to the way the pool contract is designed, Alice might be able to withdraw not only his `1 wei` but also Bob's whole deposit.

This can be replayed multiple times until the depositors notice the problem

The first depositor can be front run by an attacker and as a result will lose a considerable part of the shares provided.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

UniswapV2 fixed this with two types of protection:

[First](https://github.com/Uniswap/v2-core/blob/master/contracts/UniswapV2Pair.sol#L119-L121), on the first mint it actually mints the first 1000 shares to the zero address.

[Second](https://github.com/Uniswap/v2-core/blob/ee547b17853e71ed4e0101ccfd52e70d5acded58/contracts/UniswapV2Pair.sol#L125), it requires that the minted shares are not 0.

Implementing them both will resolve this vulnerability.





## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/markets/spot/SpotMarket.sol#L216-L219


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The function that handles the swap of quote and base tokens checks the balance of the contract for each of the tokens, which can be manipulated with a small donation, leading to a revert and therefore a `Denial of Service`.

## Proof of Concept

When the function [executeOrder](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/markets/spot/SpotMarket.sol#L85-L92) in [SpotMarket](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/markets/spot/SpotMarket.sol) gets called, it calls its internal function, which in turn calls [_swap](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/markets/spot/SpotMarket.sol#L206-L226). The [_swap](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/markets/spot/SpotMarket.sol#L206-L226) function makes sure that the reserves of both the `quote` and `base` tokens remain accurate after a settlement is executed. That same settlement takes place due to the call to [_execSettlement](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/markets/spot/SpotMarket.sol#L228-L247), which poses a risk of the reserves getting updated inaccurately. Because of this, the balance before and after the call is saved in variables, however, there’s an issue in the way the balances are got after the settlement:
```solidity
 …
    _execSettlement(spotOrder.quoteToken, spotOrder.baseToken, settlementParams, - totalBaseAmount);

    uint256 afterQuoteReserve = ERC20(spotOrder.quoteToken).balanceOf(address(this));
 @> uint256 afterBaseReserve = ERC20(spotOrder.baseToken).balanceOf(address(this));
 …
```
By directly checking the balance of each token with `balanceOf(address(this))`, a malicious user could back-run the call to `_execSettlement` by donating `1 wei` to the base token balance. The small discrepancy of `1 wei` would make the following [check](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/markets/spot/SpotMarket.sol#L221-L223) revert:
```solidity
 if (totalBaseAmount + baseReserve.toInt256() != afterBaseReserve.toInt256()) {
  revert BaseCurrencyNotSettled();
 }
```

The flow of the attack is simple, imagine the following scenario:
1. Alice notices a fluctuation in the prices, so she creates a new order.
2. After [executeOrder](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/markets/spot/SpotMarket.sol#L85-L92) is called, the logic behind opening a new position is being executed.
3. Bob spots the call to `_execSettlement` and back-runs it by donating `1 wei` to the `base` token balance of the contract.
4. The call reverts, and Alice has her strategy broken.

This could be repeated numerous times, as `1 wei` is such a miniscule amount that it wouldn’t cost anything for Bob to deny Alice for however long he wants to.

As a conclusion: a bot could be set up in such a way that multiple calls could be reverted with a small amount of `1 wei`, which breaks one of the core functionalities of the `SpotMarket` contract.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

For this issue to be resolved, a mapping within the `SpotMarket` contract should be created that tracks its balance for both the quote and base tokens, which would only be increased by internal calls in the contract.


## Assessed type

MEV

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/settlements/UniswapSettlement.sol#L22


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`block.timestamp` is used as the deadline for swap in [UniswapSettlement::swapExactMin()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/settlements/UniswapSettlement.sol#L22C3-L36C6) 

In the PoS model, proposers know well in advance if they will propose one or consecutive blocks ahead of time. In such a scenario, a malicious validator can hold back the transaction and execute it at a more favourable block number. 

This basically disables the transaction expiration check because the deadline will be set to whatever timestamp the block including the transaction is minted at.

## Proof of Concept

```solidity
function swapExactIn(
        address,
        address baseToken,
        bytes memory data,
        uint256 amountIn,
        uint256 amountOutMinimum,
        address recipient
) external override returns (uint256 amountOut) {
        ERC20(baseToken).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amountIn);
        ERC20(baseToken).approve(address(_swapRouter), amountIn);

        amountOut = _swapRouter.exactInput(
            ISwapRouter.ExactInputParams(data, recipient, block.timestamp, amountIn, amountOutMinimum)
        );
    }

```

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider a reasonable value to the deadline argument. For example, [Uniswap sets it to 30 minutes on the Ethereum mainnet and to 5 minutes on L2 networks](https://github.com/Uniswap/interface/blob/main/apps/web/src/constants/misc.ts#L9C1-L10C43) or allow the function caller to specify the swap deadline input parameter.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L206


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The spot price(slot0) of the pool, can be easily manipulated through a flashloan and thus could return a highly inaccurate result.

## Proof of Concept

The spot price is used to calculate the in-range liquidity reallocation:

The Reallocator contract initiates the rebalancing process by calling [PredyPool::reallocate()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L251C1-L258C1), which in turn calls [ReallocationLogic::reallocate()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/logic/ReallocationLogic.sol#L27).

This function takes global data, a pair ID, and settlement data as input. It then calls the [Perp contract's reallocate function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/logic/ReallocationLogic.sol#L49) with relevant parameters and returns whether the in-range liquidity changed.

This contract [retrieves the `currentSqrtPrice` from the UniswapV3 pool's slot0 data](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L206).

[`currentSqrtPrice` is used if the current tick is out of range](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L254C7-L257C10). If so, the [Perp::swapForOutOfRange()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L305) function is called to swap tokens and adjust the liquidity positions:

In [Perp::swapForOutOfRange()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L305) the`_currentSqrtPrice`is used to calculate the`deltaPosition0`and the`deltaPosition1` through [LPMath::calculateAmount0ForLiquidity()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/math/LPMath.sol#L30) and [LPMath::calculateAmount1ForLiquidity()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/math/LPMath.sol#L68) functions.

The [Perp contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol) doesn't have any checks against the price (it doesn't use any oracles nor the TWAP), so each token liquidity is manipulable through flash loans.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L202C3-L206C114

```solidity
/src/libraries/Perp.sol

202: function reallocate(
203:         DataType.PairStatus storage _assetStatusUnderlying,
204:         SqrtPerpAssetStatus storage _sqrtAssetStatus
205:     ) internal returns (bool, bool, int256 deltaPositionBase, int256 deltaPositionQuote) {
206:         (uint160 currentSqrtPrice, int24 currentTick,,,,,) = IUniswapV3Pool(_sqrtAssetStatus.uniswapPool).slot0();
```

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider using the TWAP price instead of the spot price.


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Trade.sol#L113
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/UniHelper.sol#L13-L15


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The  [Trade contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Trade.sol) lacks any checks against the retrieved price. It doesn't utilize TWAP. Consequently, an attacker can manipulate the spot price (slot0) through a flash loan attack. This manipulation can lead to highly inaccurate trade results and potential loss of funds for the users.

## Proof of Concept

The [Trade contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Trade.sol)  initiates the trading process by calling  [Trade::trade()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Trade.sol#L32). This function sets the `tradeResult.sqrtPrice` by calling [Trade::getSqrtPrice()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Trade.sol#L49).

The [Trade::getSqrtPrice()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Trade.sol#L49) retrieves the `sqrtPrice` using the `uniswapPool` and the boolean  `isQuoteZero` as arguments.

Internally calls the [UniHelper::getSqrtPrice()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Trade.sol#L113) function with the relevant parameters and returns the `sqrtPrice` calculated directly [using the spot price(slot0)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/UniHelper.sol#L14), which an attacker can manipulate, which can lead to highly inaccurate trade results and potential loss of funds for the users.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Trade.sol#L112C5-L114C6

```solidity
/src/libraries/Trade.sol

112: function getSqrtPrice(address uniswapPoolAddress, bool isQuoteZero) internal view returns (uint256 sqrtPriceX96) {
113:         return UniHelper.convertSqrtPrice(UniHelper.getSqrtPrice(uniswapPoolAddress), isQuoteZero);
114:     }
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/UniHelper.sol#L13C4-L15C6

```solidity
/src/libraries/UniHelper.sol

13:   function getSqrtPrice(address uniswapPoolAddress) internal view returns (uint160 sqrtPrice) {
14:        (sqrtPrice,,,,,,) = IUniswapV3Pool(uniswapPoolAddress).slot0();
15:   }
```

### Coded PoC

In order to run the test, go to `test/pool` and replace the content of `Trade.t.sol` with the one from the gist below. You can also delete the file and create a new one with its code.

https://gist.github.com/Vancelott/198c4e9133a7ee5d4d6900471a9717f7

Basic flow of the test:
1. Alice wants to initiate a trade in a specific pair.
2. After that, she simply calls [trade](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Trade.sol#L32).
3. A malicious user (Bob) tracks the protocol's mempool and notices the call.
4. Bob takes out a flash loan and adds liquidity to the Uniswap pool associated with the pair in Predy.
5. As the spot price is used within the calculations of the trade, Alice has traded for less tokens due to Bob's added liquidity.
6. Bob then withdraws his liquidity and pays back the flash loan.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider using the TWAP price instead of the spot price in order to prevent price manipulation.





## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L109-L111


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

As the protocol’s current intent is to use `WETH, USDC, ARB, USDT, DAI, WBTC`, it is evident that they wouldn’t want other tokens to be added as pairs. With improper validation, it is completely possible for any user to add any token that is supported by `Uniswap`.

## Proof of Concept

The current implementation of the protocol has `PredyPool`’s function [registerPair](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L109-L111) limited to only be called by users with the [operator](https://docs.predy.finance/predy-v6/dev/architecture#operator-poolcreator) role, however, it [was confirmed](https://discord.com/channels/810916927919620096/1242872233345679501/1245440813144477707) that any user would be able to create pairs. Therefore, once users have access to the function, they will be able to create a pair with any token they desire, as long as it’s available on `Uniswap`. At the moment, there’s no way for the protocol to differentiate the allowed tokens from the disallowed ones, thereby enabling users to use all other tokens besides `WETH, USDC, ARB, USDT, DAI, WBTC`.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

In order for the issue to be mitigated, a mapping with the whitelisted tokens should be created, which would restrict users from creating pairs with tokens outside of it.





## Assessed type

Other

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L251-L257
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L206


# Vulnerability details

The spot price is used to calculate the in-range liquidity reallocation:

The Reallocator contract initiates the rebalancing process by calling [PredyPool::reallocate()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L251C1-L258C1), which in turn calls [ReallocationLogic::reallocate()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/logic/ReallocationLogic.sol#L27).

This function takes global data, a pair ID, and settlement data as input. It then calls the [Perp contract's reallocate function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/logic/ReallocationLogic.sol#L49) with relevant parameters and returns whether the in-range liquidity changed.

This contract [retrieves the `currentSqrtPrice` from the UniswapV3 pool's slot0 data](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L206).

[`currentSqrtPrice` is used if the current tick is out of range](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L254C7-L257C10). If so, the [Perp::swapForOutOfRange()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L305) function is called to swap tokens and adjust the liquidity positions:

In [Perp::swapForOutOfRange()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L305) the `_currentSqrtPrice` is used to calculate the `deltaPosition0` and the `deltaPosition1` through [LPMath::calculateAmount0ForLiquidity()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/math/LPMath.sol#L30) and [LPMath::calculateAmount1ForLiquidity()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/math/LPMath.sol#L68) functions.

The [Perp contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/libraries/Perp.sol) doesn't have any checks against the price (it doesn't use any oracles nor the TWAP), so each token liquidity is manipulable through flash loans.

## Impact

The [Reallocation flow](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L251C4-L257C6) in the Predy Pool contract is susceptible to manipulation due to the lack of any checks against the retrieved in-range liquidity. It doesn't utilize TWAP. Consequently, an attacker can manipulate the spot price (slot0) through a flash loan attack. This manipulation can lead to highly inaccurate results and potential loss of funds for the users.

## Proof of Concept

Coded PoC: https://gist.github.com/cholakovvv/43fa4630fc7f62b80b11075aea279e12

Basic flow of the test:
1. Alice wants to reallocate a specific pair.
2. After that, she simply calls [PredyPool::reallocate()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/main/src/PredyPool.sol#L251C4-L257C6).
3. A malicious user (Bob) tracks the protocol's mempool and notices the call.
4. Bob takes out a flash loan and adds liquidity to the Uniswap pool associated with the pair in Predy.
5. As the spot price is used within the calculations of the reallocation, Alice get a bigger in-range due to Bob's added liquidity.
6. Bob then withdraws his liquidity and pays back the flash loan.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider using the TWAP price instead of the spot price in order to prevent price manipulation.





## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/base/BaseMarket.sol#L42
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/base/BaseMarketUpgradable.sol#L91
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/PredyPool.sol#L254
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/logic/ReallocationLogic.sol#L27
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/Perp.sol#L202


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Any external integrations that depends on the bool parameter risks being fed wrong data upon querying the `reallocate` function. This is because the function expects to return the `relocationOccurred` bool where as the internally queried `reallocate` function returns the `isRangeChanged` function instead. This can lead to unexpected reversions in these integrations, potential loss of funds, and poor user experience if active users continuosly trying to reallocate but keep getting showed the wrong information, or not believing that reallocation has occured when it infact hasn't, i.e silent reallocation failures.

BaseMarket.sol
```solidity
    function reallocate(uint256 pairId, IFillerMarket.SettlementParams memory settlementParams)
        external
        returns (bool relocationOccurred)
    {
        return _predyPool.reallocate(pairId, _getSettlementData(settlementParams));
    }
```
BaseMarketUpgradable.sol
```solidity
    function reallocate(uint256 pairId, IFillerMarket.SettlementParamsV3 memory settlementParams)
        external
        returns (bool relocationOccurred)
    {
        return _predyPool.reallocate(pairId, _getSettlementDataFromV3(settlementParams, msg.sender));
    }
```

The two contracts above call the `reallocate` function in PredyPool.sol which calls `reallocate` in  ReallocationLogic.sol
```solidity
    function reallocate(uint256 pairId, bytes memory settlementData)
        external
        nonReentrant
        returns (bool relocationOccurred)
    {
        return ReallocationLogic.reallocate(globalData, pairId, settlementData);
    }
```
In ReallocationLogic.sol, the `isRangeChanged` bool is returned instead, causing that information fed to the contracts above will be the status of the `isRangedChanged` rather than `relocationOccurred`.
```solidity
    function reallocate(GlobalDataLibrary.GlobalData storage globalData, uint256 pairId, bytes memory settlementData)
        external
        returns (bool isRangeChanged)
    {
```

## Proof of Concept

This [gist](https://gist.github.com/ZanyBonzy/a6912b57902e45544e66277fde8ed27e)  provides a short POC that can be deployed and tested on [remix](https://remix.ethereum.org/).

## Tools Used
Manual code review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change the `reallocate` function in ReallocationLogic.sol as belows.
 ```solidity
    function reallocate(GlobalDataLibrary.GlobalData storage globalData, uint256 pairId, bytes memory settlementData)
        external
        returns (bool relocationOccurred)
    {
```


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/PriceFeed.sol#L35 # Vulnerability details ## Impact The price feed hardcodes the valid time period to about 300 seconds which is bad for two reasons. 1. The hardocded value is incorrect for arbitrum, too large, allowing for stale prices to be used. 2. Considering that the protocol aims to deploy to different chains, the pyth declared valid time period for the chains can be different, and hardcoding risks beiung too small on certain chains and too large on others which can lead to a host of unexpected behaviours. Use of stale prices risks the protocol working with incorrect pricing will affect a lot of the protocol operations. ## Proof of Concept From PriceFeed.sol, the valid time period is hardcoded to `5 * 60`; ```solidity uint256 private constant VALID_TIME_PERIOD = 5 * 60; ``` This is then used to in the `getSqrtPrice` function, in `getPriceNoOlderThan` functions. ```solidity function getSqrtPrice() external view returns (uint256 sqrtPrice) { (, int256 quoteAnswer,,,) = AggregatorV3Interface(_quotePriceFeed).latestRoundData(); IPyth.Price memory basePrice = IPyth(_pyth).getPriceNoOlderThan(_priceId, VALID_TIME_PERIOD); ....... ``` However, the hardcoded valid time period is too large for arbitrum. According to pyth [docs](https://docs.pyth.network/price-feeds/api-reference/evm/configuration), the valid time period for arbitrum is 60 seconds.

Also according to the getprice [evm reference](https://github.com/pyth-network/documentation/blob/f9e61d6948a2142888550117e5023bc6479219f9/pages/price-feeds/api-reference/evm/get-price.mdx#get-price) > This function reverts with a StalePrice error if the on-chain price has not been updated within the last getValidTimePeriod() seconds. The default valid time period is set to a reasonable default on each chain and is typically around 1 minute. This means that price updates later than the reasonable default of 60 seconds will be accepted which will already be stale. This is used to get the `sqrtPrice` in the `getSqrtPrice` function. The function is extensively in the protocol to calculate `getSqrtIndexPrice` and to [calculate min margin](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/libraries/PositionCalculator.sol#L75) which helps check for a position's liquidatable state. It's also used in gamma market to [`autoHedge`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/gamma/GammaTradeMarket.sol#L237), [`autoClose`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/gamma/GammaTradeMarket.sol#L286) and to do [both](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/gamma/GammaTradeMarket.sol#L346). It's also used in [PerpMarketV1 contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-predy/blob/a9246db5f874a91fb71c296aac6a66902289306a/src/markets/perp/PerpMarketV1.sol#L227) Also, as the protocol aims to deploy on Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, the hardcoded value might be too low for Base and Optimism(no concrete info could be found). This will cause unexpected reversions as price updates time are much higher than the hardcoded time, thus causing actual valid prices to be rejected as being stale. ## Tools Used Manual code review ## Recommended Mitigation Steps Recommend setting the value in the constructor, upon deployment to match each chain and it's needed value. ## Assessed type Other
